sections.heading: Asking for the grace this day will need
sections.text: Father, every good thing comes from you. I’m coming to you at the start of this day because I don’t yet know all that it will ask of me, but you do. Give me the grace I will need for the work, conversations, decisions, interruptions, and surprises ahead.
theological_themes: God is the source of all good, and daily obedience depends on fresh grace from him.
The day is received from God, not controlled by me.

scripture_references.connection: James teaches that every good gift comes from the Father, which grounds the prayer’s opening dependence on God as the giver of all needed good.
The passage invites believers to come to God for mercy and timely grace, fitting the prayer’s request for help before the needs of the day arrive.

sections.heading: Knowing my weakness before I step into the day
sections.text: As I go into a broken world, I know I’m not only facing trouble outside me; I also carry sin inside me. Without you, I cannot bear lasting fruit or stay faithful. Even ordinary things that look harmless can become traps for pride, selfishness, anger, or foolishness if you do not keep me. Hold me up today, and keep me safe in you.
theological_themes: Human weakness is both external and internal: the world is fallen, and the heart is prone to sin.
Perseverance and faithfulness depend on God’s keeping power.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus says that fruitful living is impossible apart from him, directly supporting the prayer’s confession that daily faithfulness cannot be produced by self-reliance.
Peter describes believers as guarded by God’s power through faith, which fits the plea to be upheld and kept safe by God.

sections.heading: Guarding my mind, loves, conduct, and witness
sections.text: Protect my mind from clever error that sounds true but leads me away from you. Protect my loves from turning created things into idols. Protect my life from choices that would stain my character. Protect my witness from anything that would dishonor the name of Christ. Keep me from doing anything today where I could not honestly ask for your blessing or welcome your searching gaze.
theological_themes: God’s holiness calls for integrity in thought, affection, conduct, and public witness.
Sin often disguises itself, so believers need God’s preserving grace and honest self-examination.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers to test what they receive, reject evil, and be sanctified wholly, matching the prayer’s concern for mind, conduct, and integrity before God.
John’s warning against idols supports the prayer’s request that the heart’s loves be kept from giving created things the place that belongs to God alone.

sections.heading: Receiving success or disappointment from your hand
sections.text: Bless what is right for me to do today. Let my work succeed if that is good, and if disappointment comes, prepare me to receive it without bitterness. Keep me from both desperation and self-sufficiency. Give me what I need—no more and no less than your wisdom appoints—so that comfort does not make me forget you, and need does not tempt me to sin against you.
theological_themes: God’s providence governs both fruitful outcomes and disappointments.
Contentment asks God for what is fitting, resisting both arrogant abundance and desperate unbelief.

scripture_references.connection: This passage asks God for neither poverty nor riches but suitable provision, because both extremes can bring spiritual danger; it is the direct biblical pattern behind this request.
James corrects presumption about future plans and teaches dependence on the Lord’s will, which supports asking God to prosper lawful work or prepare the heart for disappointment.

sections.heading: Using what you give without misusing it
sections.text: Teach me to receive your gifts with prayer and gratitude, and to use this world without being ruled by it. Help me make good use of the abilities you have entrusted to me. Help me not waste the time you give. Make me wise and gracious toward people who do not yet know you. Give me a ready heart to do good to everyone I can, especially to my brothers and sisters in Christ. And in all of it, Father, let the credit and praise belong to you.
theological_themes: Created gifts are good when received under God’s Word, prayer, and will.
Christian stewardship includes time, abilities, public wisdom, love for neighbors, and special care for fellow believers.
All faithful living is finally for God’s glory.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that God’s created gifts are to be received with thanksgiving and set apart by God’s Word and prayer, which supports the prayer’s request to use creation rightly.
Paul urges believers to walk carefully and make the best use of time, grounding the prayer’s concern to redeem the day rather than waste it.
This passage calls Christians to do good to all, with particular care for the household of faith, matching the prayer’s closing movement toward active love.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s phrase “a wicked world” can sound as if evil is only outside the believer. The adaptation preserves the fallen-world emphasis while also keeping the original’s immediate confession of an evil heart within the praying person.

The request for “neither poverty nor riches” reflects Proverbs 30:8-9 and assumes material extremes can bring spiritual temptations; this may need pastoral sensitivity for readers experiencing poverty, but the biblical concern has been preserved.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Profession” was rendered as “witness” and “the name of Christ” because the original likely means the believer’s public confession and reputation as a Christian, not employment or vocation.
“Every creature” was interpreted in the older sense of created thing or created gift, so the adaptation speaks of receiving and using God’s gifts with prayer and gratitude.
“Use the world, and not abuse it” was rendered as using the world without being ruled by it, preserving the older moral sense of rightly handling created goods without turning them into idols.
